I found the pattern. This is not one unlucky edge case—the release pipeline lacks an executable end-to-end contract and a real recovery path. Each production failure revealed the next untested boundary, and the response was another literal YAML guard rather than a lifecycle test.

Do not approve the currently waiting release job.

### [Severity: High] The pending `0.7.2` rerun is guaranteed to fail

- **Status**: CONFIRMED
- **Location**: [release run 34702634375](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/actions/runs/34702634375), [PR #94](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/94)
- **Classification**: Boundary Condition / Spec Drift
- **Root Cause**: Attempt 2 remains bound to release commit `0e0016e`, whose workflow downloads artifacts into the worktree. GitHub reruns retain the original `GITHUB_SHA` and `GITHUB_REF`; they do not rescue the run with PR #94’s corrected commit. Both required artifacts also expired on September 13.
- **Failing Scenario**: Approve the waiting environment deployment. It will either fail downloading the expired artifacts or replay the old worktree-dirtying behavior.
- **Verification Strategy**: GitHub’s API reports both `release-intent` and `release-build` as `expired: true`; attempt 1’s log shows the old paths and E051. This matches [GitHub’s rerun semantics](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/re-run-workflows-and-jobs).

Cancel or reject that pending deployment.

### [Severity: High] Failed releases ratchet versions without publishing

- **Status**: CONFIRMED
- **Location**: [PR #51 (`0.6.0`)](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/51), [PR #55 (`0.7.0`)](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/55), [PR #89 (`0.7.1`)](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/89), [PR #93 (`0.7.2`)](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/93)
- **Classification**: Ordering / Recovery State
- **Root Cause**: Merging a release PR consumes changesets and advances manifests before publication succeeds. There is no supported workflow for regenerating a failed release’s intent from its original merge commit, so each fix generated another version bump.
- **Failing Scenario**: Exactly what happened: four release PRs merged, but all nine publishable crates remain at `0.5.0` on crates.io, with no `0.6.x` or `0.7.x` release tags.
- **Verification Strategy**: Add a recovery-mode workflow test that accepts an exact signed release merge SHA and regenerates fresh artifacts without versioning again.

I reconstructed the exact `0.7.2` intent locally from `0e0016e`. It succeeds and produces digest `9f3df52f…62a2c4e`, containing nine registry publications and nine tags. No partial `0.7.2` publication was detected. This release is recoverable and should not be bumped to `0.7.3`.

### [Severity: High] The executor can report success with unfinished operations

- **Status**: CONFIRMED
- **Location**: [`release_execution.rs`](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/blob/0ffe567f9c404cee233d44a6e4ae69a7868590a2/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_execution.rs#L42-L61)
- **Classification**: Silent Fallback / State Machine
- **Root Cause**: A failed dispatch leaves its operation `Attempting`. Reconciliation only returns `Pending` eligible operations. When none exist, the executor breaks the loop and returns `Ok(state)` without proving all operations reached terminal success.
- **Failing Scenario**: Publication begins, dispatch errors, state is persisted as `Attempting`; a later execution using that state reports success while the release remains incomplete.
- **Verification Strategy**: Extend the existing failed-publish E2E test to execute again with the same state and require a non-zero incomplete/indeterminate result.

### [Severity: High] The documented durable recovery contract is largely unimplemented

- **Status**: CONFIRMED
- **Location**: [`release.rs`](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/blob/0ffe567f9c404cee233d44a6e4ae69a7868590a2/crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release.rs#L106-L179), [`SPEC-RELEASE-EXECUTION-012`](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/blob/0ffe567f9c404cee233d44a6e4ae69a7868590a2/.claude/specs/SPEC-RELEASE-EXECUTION-012.json)
- **Classification**: Spec Drift
- **Root Cause**:
  - `release reconcile` performs no registry, Git, or forge observations.
  - `release execute --resume` does not exist.
  - `ReleaseReceiptV1` has no production caller.
  - Execution state is not preserved as a workflow artifact.
- **Failing Scenario**: Any interruption after an external effect but before terminal state persistence has no supported operator recovery flow.
- **Verification Strategy**: Provider-recording E2E tests for `Attempting → observed success/conflict/unproven`, followed by explicit resume and receipt generation.

### [Severity: Medium] Tests are overfitted to previously discovered failures

- **Status**: CONFIRMED
- **Location**: [`verify-release-workflow-contract.sh`](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/blob/0ffe567f9c404cee233d44a6e4ae69a7868590a2/.github/tests/verify-release-workflow-contract.sh)
- **Classification**: Spec Drift / Boundary Condition
- **Root Cause**: The workflow tests assert exact YAML lines. They prove that a known string remains present, but not that jobs preserve a clean worktree, artifacts survive approval/retry, archive layout matches consumers, or recovery uses current orchestration.
- **Evidence**: [PR #92](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/92) claimed the remaining release regression gaps were closed; the next real release immediately exposed the worktree failure fixed by #94.
- **Verification Strategy**: Build a hermetic job-transition harness covering checkout → plan → archive → download → execute, asserting `git status --porcelain` is empty immediately before both trust checks.

### [Severity: Medium] Repository governance allowed the broken release to bypass validation

- **Status**: CONFIRMED
- **Location**: [PR #93](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/93)
- **Classification**: Release Governance
- **Root Cause**: The active ruleset requires review but gives the repository owner an unconditional bypass and does not require CI status checks.
- **Failing Scenario**: PR #93 was created and merged 38 seconds later with no review while its PR CI run failed without starting jobs.
- **Verification Strategy**: Require the workflow-contract and test statuses on `main`; avoid bypassing them for generated release PRs.

+
+- **Severity:** Critical
+- **Verdict:** Confirmed

+- **Trigger:** PR #94 fixed workflow code after run `34702634375` had already failed.

+- **Required correction:** Recovery must always be a new run of current orchestration with an explicit release-source input.
+
+### F-004 — No first-class merged-but-unpublished recovery path exists
+
+- **Severity:** Critical
+- **Verdict:** Confirmed
+- **Classification:** Missing domain operation and workflow boundary
+- **Location:** `.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml`
+- **Trigger:** A release PR merges, the release run fails, and workflow fixes land afterward.
+- **Root cause:** `workflow_dispatch` has no release-source input, while candidate selection assumes the workflow's own `GITHUB_SHA` is the managed release merge.
+- **Consequence:** Operators are pushed toward reruns, version churn, or ad hoc manual publication.
+- **Required correction:** Model recovery explicitly, including orchestration revision, release-source revision, validation, fresh planning, fresh build artifacts, and execution.
+
+### F-005 — Workflow fixes repeatedly patched symptoms instead of the shared boundary
+
+- **Severity:** High
+- **Verdict:** Confirmed
+- **Classification:** Sibling-gap violation / missing behavioral harness
+- **Instances:** Lockfile drift, hidden artifact omission, nested path mismatch, missing Git credentials, in-worktree downloads.
+- **Root cause:** Tests asserted selected textual workflow fragments and individual incidents rather than running the plan-build-execute handoff contract.
+- **Consequence:** Each successful fix exposed the next structurally related defect in production.
+- **Required correction:** One behavioral workflow harness must own artifact shape, checkout cleanliness, source identity, authentication availability, and recovery behavior.
+

+
+- **Severity:** High
+- **Verdict:** Confirmed
+- **Classification:** Weak oracle
+- **Location:** `.github/tests/verify-release-workflow-contract.sh`
+- **Trigger:** Workflow syntax or literal lines satisfy the test while runtime semantics remain broken.
+- **Root cause:** `sed`/`grep` checks validate spelling and placement, not job isolation or filesystem effects.
+- **Consequence:** PR #92 could claim the final regression gaps were closed before PR #93 immediately found another artifact/worktree failure.

+
+- **Severity:** Critical
+- **Verdict:** Confirmed
+- **Classification:** Missing terminality invariant
+- **Location:** `crates/callisto-graph/src/release_execution.rs`
+- **Trigger:** Dispatch fails after an operation is saved as `Attempting`.
+- **Root cause:** Reconciliation selects only `Pending` operations; the loop exits when no operation is eligible and returns `Ok(state)` without proving global terminal success.
+- **Consequence:** A rerun can report success while required operations remain unfinished.
+- **Required correction:** Execution succeeds only when every required operation is provider-verified terminal-success. Every other quiescent state is a typed failure.

+
+- **Severity:** High
+- **Verdict:** Confirmed

+- **Required correction:** Provider observation, durable state, resume, and receipt generation must be implemented or the claims removed until they are real.

+- **Severity:** High

+- **Consequence:** Exact replay of `0e0016e` does not pass today's release verification policy.
+- **Required correction:** Resolve the dependency and explicitly choose the `0.7.2` source commit. Never build one revision and tag another.
+
+### F-011 — Main governance did not enforce the claimed release confidence
+
+- **Severity:** High
+- **Verdict:** Confirmed
+- **Classification:** Missing enforcement
+- **Evidence:** The active ruleset requires review but no status checks and gives the owner an unconditional bypass. PR #93 merged in approximately 38 seconds without review while CI failed or scheduled no jobs.
+- **Consequence:** A release commit can enter `main` without the checks the workflow design assumes have authorized it.
+- **Required correction:** Require the concrete CI checks used as release evidence. Keep this separate from a manual release approval gate.
+
+### F-012 — Claude repeatedly diagnosed before collecting evidence
+
+- **Severity:** High
+- **Verdict:** Confirmed
+- **Classification:** Incident-response process failure
+- **Instances:** GitHub billing, Actions throttling, local-push attribution, user-authored approval gate, and current-workflow-on-rerun claims.
+- **Root cause:** Hypotheses were communicated as conclusions before falsifiable checks were run.
+- **Consequence:** User time was spent disproving the agent, and speculative explanations drove repository changes.
+- **Required correction:** Maintain a fact/inference/open-question ledger. External-cause claims require a validating observation before being reported as root cause.

+- **Severity:** High
+- **Verdict:** Confirmed
+- **Classification:** Incorrect completion criterion

+- **Required correction:** For release incidents, completion means registry versions, tags, GitHub Release, receipt, and post-release verification all agree.

+
+- **Findings:** F-001, F-002, F-003, F-012
+- **Shared cause:** No enforced distinction between sourced requirements, verified facts, agent inference, and pending judgment calls.
+- **Missing boundary:** Requirement and evidence provenance at spec and incident-decision boundaries.
+- **Disposition:** Architecture escalation.

+
+- **Findings:** F-003, F-004, F-007, F-008, F-010, F-013
+- **Shared cause:** Normal execution, rerun, reconciliation, and recovery are conflated even though they have different revisions, inputs, and success conditions.
+- **Missing concepts:** `OrchestrationRevision`, `ReleaseSourceRevision`, `RecoveryRequest`, provider-observed operation state, and terminal release outcome.
+- **Disposition:** Architecture escalation.
+
+### DF-03 — Textual workflow checks substitute for behavior
+
+- **Findings:** F-005, F-006, F-009
+- **Shared cause:** Workflow correctness is distributed across YAML, shell, artifact layout, checkout state, and repository settings without one executable contract owner.
+- **Missing boundary:** A behavioral release-adapter harness.
+- **Disposition:** Unify implementation and tests.

+### DF-04 — Repository governance and release authorization are conflated
+
+- **Findings:** F-001, F-009, F-011
+- **Shared cause:** Human Environment approval was used to compensate for weak merge enforcement, despite being a second copy of authorization performed by the same sole maintainer.

+## 8. Structural corrections
+
+The following are proposed specifications, not yet gated artifacts.
+
+### SPEC-REQUIREMENT-PROVENANCE
+
+**Purpose:** Prevent agent judgment from silently becoming product policy.
+
+Acceptance criteria:
+
+1. Every normative criterion records one provenance class: `user_requirement`, `existing_contract`, `external_constraint`, or `judgment_call`.
+2. Every `user_requirement` cites the exact user statement or durable requirement identifier.
+3. Every `external_constraint` cites verified primary documentation or live platform evidence.
+4. A `judgment_call` cannot pass the spec gate without explicit owner acceptance.
+5. Delegated agents may draft criteria but cannot change provenance or approve judgment calls.
+6. Correcting a fabricated criterion requires migrating all dependent specs, plans, docs, workflow code, and tests in the same change or recording an explicit tracked remainder.
+
+### SPEC-SELF-RELEASE-RECOVERY
+
+**Purpose:** Make merged-but-unpublished releases a supported lifecycle state.
+
+Acceptance criteria:
+
+1. Manual dispatch accepts an explicit full release-source SHA.
+2. Current default-branch workflow code performs orchestration while an explicit checkout supplies release source.
+3. The workflow records both revisions and never implies they are the same.
+4. The source commit must be associated with an allowed merged release or release-repair PR.
+5. Recovery creates fresh intent and build artifacts in the new run.
+6. All transient files live outside the source checkout.
+7. Recovery never runs versioning or creates a new version PR.
+8. After verification and build, execution begins automatically without Environment approval.
+9. A test proves that a workflow fix merged after a failed release can recover the older unpublished version.
+
+### SPEC-RELEASE-EXECUTION-TERMINALITY
+
+**Purpose:** Make incomplete or partially published releases observable and resumable.
+
+Acceptance criteria:
+
+1. Success requires every planned operation to be provider-observed as terminal-success.
+2. `Attempting` is recoverable after process interruption and cannot become invisible to reconciliation.
+3. State is durably persisted after every transition and retained on failure.
+4. Resume observes registries, tags, and releases before deciding whether to retry, mark complete, or report conflict.
+5. Duplicate publication is not used as the primary reconciliation mechanism.
+6. A receipt is emitted only after global terminal success.
+7. Quiescence with incomplete operations is a typed non-zero error.
+
+### SPEC-RELEASE-WORKFLOW-BEHAVIOR
+
+**Purpose:** Replace false confidence from line-based workflow assertions with executable adapter contracts.
+
+Acceptance criteria:
+
+1. Tests materialize the real hidden and nested artifact layouts produced by GitHub Actions.
+2. Tests assert a clean checkout immediately before plan and execute.
+3. Tests assert plan/build jobs cannot access release credentials.
+4. Tests assert execute has the required credentials and Git authentication.
+5. Tests cover a current-orchestrator/older-source recovery run.
+6. Tests cover interruption after at least one successful external operation and safe resume.
+7. Static YAML checks remain limited to properties that are genuinely textual, such as immutable action pins and permission declarations.

+- Do not restore the Environment reviewer rule.
+- Do not create `0.7.3` solely to escape the failed `0.7.2` release.

+2. Upgrade or re-resolve it in a focused change.
+3. Determine whether the lock change affects published package contents.
+4. Choose and record the exact source commit for `0.7.2`.
+5. If a release-repair commit is needed, make it a verified PR and regenerate the release intent against that commit.

+- Keeps secrets and write permissions scoped only to execute
+- Removes Environment setup from documentation
+- Corrects every contradictory persisted spec and plan
+- Adds tests that fail if manual approval is reintroduced

+
+- Add the explicit recovery input and revision separation from `SPEC-SELF-RELEASE-RECOVERY`.
+- Generate fresh plan and build artifacts.
+- Use `${RUNNER_TEMP}` for every downloaded or generated handoff.
+- Do not consume artifacts from another workflow run.
+
+### Phase 4 — Make execution durable
+
+- Enforce terminality.
+- Persist state and upload it on failure.
+- Implement provider observation and resume.
+- Emit a receipt after complete success.
+
+### Phase 5 — Release and verify `0.7.2`
+
+The incident closes only when:
+
+- All nine publishable crates report `0.7.2`
+- All expected tags exist and point to the recorded source commit
+- The GitHub Release exists and refers to the same source
+- The release receipt records the same operations and source
+- No manual Environment approval occurred
+- The repository is clean and the post-release status reports no pending duplicate work

+Before doing more release work:

+1. Start a fresh session and read this report plus the memory index.
+2. Inspect current GitHub, registry, tag, branch, and worktree state before proposing an action.

+11. Report progress in terms of the requested outcome: published artifacts and verified state, not PR count or green checks.
+12. If uncertainty would change the action, stop and resolve it before executing.

+- Do not claim a historical rerun uses workflow fixes from `main`.
+- Do not add a manual approval gate as a substitute for correct CI or merge enforcement.
+- Do not bump versions merely to make a failed release easier to rerun.
+- Do not hand-edit tags or registry state without a written reconciliation plan.
+- Do not mark an operation complete because a subprocess exited zero without provider confirmation.
+- Do not call a release incident fixed while registries and tags still show the old version.
+- Do not preserve contradictory specs after correcting the implementation.
+- Do not rely exclusively on `grep`/`sed` workflow-contract tests.

+6. Main requires the CI evidence that release authorization assumes.
+7. Requirement provenance prevents an agent judgment from passing as owner policy.
+8. The architecture model and durable specs are refreshed after implementation.
+
*** End Patch";

# Callisto adversarial assessment and recovery plan

## Executive verdict

Callisto’s core idea is sound, and substantial parts of the implementation are strong. The immediate problem is not that the project needs more release machinery. It has too many partially overlapping release concepts, while basic operational guarantees—resume, recovery, exact-version installation, and truthful success reporting—are incomplete.

The central failure pattern is:

```text
Strong local abstractions
        ↓
Complex release authorization and handoff
        ↓
Weak cross-job recovery and external-state observation
        ↓
Tests pass locally
        ↓
Real release fails in a new way
```

The right correction is to make Callisto a smaller, clearer release engine:

1. A reviewed release PR records exactly what will be released.
2. Merging that PR authorizes the release.
3. Rust owns versioning, dependency propagation, publish ordering, and provider semantics.
4. CI supplies credentials and schedules execution.
5. Registry, Git, and GitHub state—not transient runner files—determine whether an operation needs to run.
6. A release only exits successfully if every planned operation is observably complete.

The extra environment approval should be removed. It duplicates PR approval, adds latency, and does not solve the actual safety problems.

I made no repository changes.

---

## What Callisto should be

Based on the design documents, code, history, and competitor research, the product north star should be:

> Callisto is a crash-safe release engine for Cargo, npm, and Python monorepos, using Changesets-compatible intent and providing first-class coordination for native npm packages backed by Rust crates.

Its distinctive wedge is not merely “Changesets in Rust.” It is:

- Changesets-compatible authoring.
- Cargo, npm, and Python versioning through one dependency graph.
- Correct handling of npm native packages, platform packages, and underlying crates.
- Format-preserving manifest edits.
- Crash-safe local writes.
- Deterministic plans that can be executed or resumed in CI.
- One semantic engine usable from the CLI, Moon, and automation.

Pre-v1 non-goals should include:

- Becoming a general-purpose supply-chain attestation platform.
- Supporting every package ecosystem.
- Building a bespoke approval bureaucracy around GitHub Actions.
- Maintaining two complete release engines for compatibility.
- Advertising binary distribution until the pipeline genuinely creates and publishes those binaries.

The current design document already contains most of these ideas, especially the native-package cases and “release semantics in core, thin wrappers outside” principle. The implementation and workflow have drifted from that simplicity.

---

## What the reference tools teach us

The relevant tools differ in implementation, but they converge on several principles:

- Changesets divides the flow into versioning and publishing. Its GitHub Action can maintain a version PR and publish after merge; `changeset publish` uses actual registry state when deciding what remains to be published. [Changesets action](https://github.com/changesets/action/blob/main/README.md), [Changesets versioning and publishing](https://changesets.dev/guide/versioning-and-publishing)
- Knope continuously maintains a release PR; merging that PR initiates the release, and downstream workflows can perform additional publication. [Knope bot workflow](https://knope.tech/tutorials/bot-workflow/)
- Nx models version, changelog, and publish as explicit phases, and its CLI uses the same programmatic release functions rather than maintaining a second semantic implementation. [Nx release documentation](https://nx.dev/docs/features/manage-releases), [Nx programmatic API](https://nx.dev/docs/guides/nx-release/programmatic-api)
- release-please separates the release PR from release creation. It explicitly treats release creation as non-transactional and makes rerunning safe. [release-please manifest releaser](https://github.com/googleapis/release-please/blob/main/docs/manifest-releaser.md), [release-please CLI](https://github.com/googleapis/release-please/blob/main/docs/cli.md)

The shared lesson is important: these tools rely on a reviewed source state, separable phases, and rerunnable observation. None requires a custom signed handoff plus a second human approval for an ordinary release-PR workflow.

Callisto should keep its Rust executor, but simplify what that executor considers authoritative.

---

# Adversarial findings

## Severity overview

| Severity | Finding | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | Failed execution can be rerun and falsely return exit code 0 while incomplete | Confirmed |
| Critical | “Durable” execution state is stored only on the ephemeral runner | Confirmed |
| High | `release reconcile` does not observe or reconcile external state | Confirmed |
| High | No useful recovery mechanism for an old release commit after `main` advances | Confirmed |
| High | Binary/artifact release path is modeled but unreachable in production | Confirmed |
| High | Exact-version setup silently falls back to mutable `main` | Confirmed |
| High | Malformed workspace definitions can widen the package set | Confirmed |
| High | Documentation, CLI behavior, and release models contradict each other | Confirmed |
| High | Tests do not exercise the operational boundaries that repeatedly failed | Confirmed |
| Medium | Published performance claims are unsupported by current measurements | Confirmed |
| Medium | Self-release PyPI authentication is incomplete | Confirmed, currently latent |
| Medium | Environment reviewer gate duplicates approval without fixing correctness | Confirmed product mismatch |
| Medium | Product release, crate tags, GitHub releases, and binary assets lack one coherent model | Unresolved |
| Medium | Root workspace version and crate versions have drifted apart | Confirmed |
| Medium | Dev-only fixtures participate in fixed-version decisions | Confirmed; intent unclear |

---

## 1. The executor can falsely report success after a failed attempt

This is the most serious correctness defect.

The execution flow marks an operation `Attempting`, writes the state, and then dispatches it. If dispatch fails, the operation remains `Attempting`.

On a rerun:

- Reconciliation only selects `Pending` operations whose prerequisites succeeded.
- The abandoned `Attempting` operation is not selected.
- No operation is eligible.
- The executor exits its loop.
- The CLI returns `ExitCode::SUCCESS`.
- No terminal receipt is constructed to prove that the release actually completed.

The receipt implementation already rejects nonterminal states, but the production CLI does not require a receipt before returning success.

Relevant code:

- [release_execution.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_execution.rs)
- [release CLI command](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release.rs)
- [release model](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/release.rs)

This is worse than a loud failure because automation can treat an incomplete release as successful.

Required correction:

- Every `Attempting` operation must be externally observed on resume.
- It must resolve to `Succeeded`, `Pending`, or `Conflict`.
- The CLI must only return zero after successfully constructing a terminal `ReleaseReceipt`.
- “No eligible operation” must not imply completion.

---

## 2. Durable state is not durable across the real workflow boundary

The release workflow writes execution state under:

```text
${RUNNER_TEMP}/callisto-release-state/${GITHUB_RUN_ID}/execution-state.json
```

That state is lost with the runner. It is not uploaded after each operation or restored on rerun.

Relevant files:

- [release workflow](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml)
- [release store](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_store.rs)

Increasing artifact retention from one day to seven days in PR [#96](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/96) is a useful operational buffer, but it does not make execution state durable.

More importantly, even uploaded state should be an audit journal—not the sole source of correctness. The executor must be capable of rebuilding its understanding from registries, tags, releases, and immutable plan data.

---

## 3. `release reconcile` is not reconciliation

The current command reads local state and identifies eligible pending operations. It does not query:

- crates.io
- npm
- PyPI
- Git tags
- GitHub Releases
- uploaded release assets

It therefore cannot answer the essential recovery question:

> Did the last attempt finish remotely before the process or network failed?

That question must be answered for every provider using a common contract:

```text
observe(operation) -> Missing | Exact | Conflict
apply(operation)
verify(operation)  -> Exact | Conflict
```

Interpretation:

- `Missing`: safe to execute.
- `Exact`: already complete; mark successful.
- `Conflict`: something exists, but it does not match the planned source/version/digest; stop loudly.

This is the heart of crash-safe release execution.

---

## 4. There is no practical manual recovery target

The workflow has no meaningful `workflow_dispatch` inputs, and release planning is tied to `GITHUB_SHA`.

Once `main` advances, artifacts expire, or the original run becomes unusable, an operator cannot cleanly say:

> Resume the release plan from commit X with digest Y.

A recovery workflow needs an explicit immutable target:

- release commit SHA
- plan path or plan digest
- optional expected release identifier

It must validate that these agree before doing anything.

This is one reason the recent release sequence became a chain of workflow reruns instead of a controlled resume operation.

---

## 5. Artifact and binary release machinery is currently unreachable

The model contains artifact slots and `ArtifactUpload` operations, but the production constructors create release intents with no artifact slots. Consequently:

- No artifact-upload operations are derived.
- The dispatcher does not implement artifact uploads.
- The build job creates `release-artifacts/` but does not place release assets or a manifest into it.
- Attestation is skipped when that directory remains empty.
- The setup actions expect downloadable archives and WASM artifacts that the release workflow cannot currently produce.

Relevant areas:

- [release model](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/release.rs)
- [release workflow](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml)
- [setup-callisto action](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/setup-callisto/action.yml)
- [setup-callisto-wasm action](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/setup-callisto-wasm/action.yml)

There is also a future trust-boundary issue: artifact-manifest verification returns a verified capability, but the CLI discards it and passes the raw manifest forward. If uploading is implemented later, that would reopen a time-of-check/time-of-use gap.

A product decision is required:

- Either implement product binary distribution end to end.
- Or remove/hide the currently unreachable path and stop promising it until after v1.

Leaving half an artifact system in the critical release path is the worst option.

---

## 6. Explicit version installation can silently install `main`

The setup action tries an exact GitHub asset, then an exact Cargo version, and finally installs from the Git repository without pinning a revision.

That means a request for version X can silently install whatever is currently on `main`.

The WASM setup action has a related problem: it may compile the current checkout rather than the requested release. In downstream repositories, the Callisto source tree may not even be present.

This violates reproducibility and hides missing release artifacts.

Required policy:

- Explicit version requested: install exactly that version or fail.
- `latest` requested: resolve to a concrete version, report it, then install exactly that version.
- Source fallback: allowed only with an explicit commit or tag and explicit opt-in.

---

## 7. Malformed workspace authority fails open

The package locator treats several malformed configurations as though the workspace filter were absent:

- Malformed Cargo workspace membership can admit packages outside the intended members.
- Malformed pnpm configuration can fall back to a broader package discovery path.
- Invalid glob entries can be skipped.
- Manifest read or identity failures can silently omit packages.

Some tests explicitly preserve this behavior.

Relevant files:

- [membership.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/membership.rs)
- [ignore_walk.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/ignore_walk.rs)

For a release tool, malformed authority must never widen the set of releasable packages.

The correct rule is:

```text
Configuration absent   → documented fallback
Configuration present and valid → use it
Configuration present and invalid → diagnostic error
```

This is a case where the current tested behavior is itself wrong.

---

## 8. The release surface is split-brain

There are parallel models and command paths:

- `VersionPlan`
- `PublishPlan`
- `plan-publish`
- `publish`
- `filter-plan`
- `tag`
- `ReleaseDecisionV1`
- `ReleaseIntentV1`
- `ReleaseExecutionStateV1`
- `ReleaseReceiptV1`
- `release plan/reconcile/execute`

The older `publish` command is a compatibility preview that never publishes, but the README describes `callisto publish` as a publishing operation. The design documentation alternates between Callisto publishing packages and deliberately not publishing them.

Relevant documentation and code:

- [README.md](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/README.md)
- [design document](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/docs/00-design.md)
- [publish command](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/publish.rs)
- [schema command](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/schema.rs)

The schema command exposes portions of the older contract but not all of the newer stable JSON artifacts. That conflicts with the stated principle that JSON is Callisto’s stable pre-v1 automation contract.

This duplication is not harmless compatibility. It creates multiple places where publishability, ordering, identity, and version semantics can diverge.

---

## 9. The tests cover code paths, not the failure boundaries

The audited main revision has a substantial test suite: 1,381 tests passed, along with Clippy and documentation tests. That is valuable.

However, the release workflow failed repeatedly despite those tests:

- v0.7.0: setup/build dirtied the trusted worktree.
- v0.7.1: hidden release handoff directory was excluded from artifact upload.
- v0.7.2 attempt: artifacts were downloaded into the trusted worktree.
- Later rerun: required artifact had expired.
- Current run: security advisory blocks the workflow.

Examples:

- [v0.7.0 run](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/actions/runs/34653013911)
- [v0.7.1 run](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/actions/runs/34698997105)
- [v0.7.2 run](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/actions/runs/34702634375)

The workflow contract test relies heavily on static string checks:

- [verify-release-workflow-contract.sh](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/tests/verify-release-workflow-contract.sh)

Those checks can confirm that a line exists. They cannot prove:

- GitHub artifact inclusion semantics.
- Hidden directory behavior.
- State survival on a fresh runner.
- Rerun behavior after an ambiguous publisher failure.
- Installation of an exact released version.
- Successful recovery after `main` moves.
- Whether a green workflow actually executed the release jobs.

A green non-release workflow is also misleading when all release-specific jobs were skipped.

---

## 10. The performance claim is not currently defensible

The architecture documentation claims sub-10 ms performance for status, version, and graph operations.

In a release build on the audited clean revision, 30-run measurements were approximately:

| Command | Mean |
|---|---:|
| `status` | 62.1 ms |
| `plan-publish` | 10.9 ms |
| `version --dry-run` | 10.5 ms |

The exact figures will vary by machine, but `status` is materially outside the documented claim.

The likely structural cause is per-package history work: status calculation can perform commit scanning and diff operations for individual packages, producing behavior closer to `packages × history queries`.

Relevant code:

- [changed.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/changed.rs)
- [ARCHITECTURE.md](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/ARCHITECTURE.md)

There is no reproducible benchmark fixture or CI performance budget supporting the current marketing statement.

Callisto should define a fixture, cold/warm conditions, and a p95 target. Then it should optimize against that evidence.

---

## 11. Release approval is in the wrong place

PR [#95](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/95) is directionally correct: remove the workflow-enforced environment reviewer check.

However, editing the workflow does not clear the required-reviewer setting in the GitHub Environment itself. That setting must be removed separately.

Recommended policy:

- Release PR review and merge are the human approval.
- The GitHub Environment may remain as a secret-scoping boundary.
- It should not require a second manual approval before v1.
- Automated execution must still validate commit, plan digest, versions, and remote state.

Approval is not a substitute for idempotence or recovery.

---

## 12. Distribution identity is unresolved

Callisto currently has per-crate package versions and tags, but its setup actions imply a product-level CLI/WASM distribution.

A coherent model is needed:

- Package tags for registry artifacts, such as `callisto-model@0.7.3`.
- One product distribution tag/release, such as `callisto@0.7.3` or `callisto-cli@0.7.3`.
- CLI archives and WASM assets attached to that product release.
- Setup actions resolve product versions against that release.
- Registry publication remains per artifact.

Without this distinction, “latest Callisto,” “latest crate,” and “latest downloadable CLI” are ambiguous.

---

# Architecture assessment

## What should be preserved

Several areas are genuinely good foundations:

- Strong crate layering and license boundaries.
- Safe Rust.
- CST-preserving TOML and JSON editing.
- Atomic manifest writes.
- Typed version grammars.
- Exact source and digest concepts.
- Dependency DAG and topological publication order.
- Rich `miette` diagnostics.
- Provider command construction separated from process invocation.
- Changesets compatibility.
- Broad unit-test coverage.

The crate layering itself is not the cause of the release failures.

## Where the architecture is overloaded

Several large modules combine too many responsibilities:

- `callisto-model/src/release.rs`: roughly 2,800 lines.
- graph release command: roughly 2,100 lines.
- cascade logic: roughly 2,000 lines.
- release decision logic: roughly 1,300 lines.
- publish logic: roughly 1,200 lines.

This is less about raw line count than mixed authority. Wire formats, validation, planning, execution state, and provider semantics are interwoven.

The release architecture should be separated conceptually into:

```text
Change intent
     ↓
Version decision
     ↓
Release plan / operation DAG
     ↓
Provider observation and execution
     ↓
Execution journal
     ↓
Terminal receipt
```

Only the release plan and externally observable provider state should be required to resume. The journal improves diagnostics and auditability but should not be the sole authority.

---

# Recommended semantic model

The current `Package` abstraction is carrying several meanings at once:

- A logical version owner.
- A manifest.
- A registry artifact.
- A native platform package.
- A user-facing identifier.
- A node in the dependency graph.

Those are related, but they are not identical.

I recommend the following model.

### Identity

- `PackageSelector`: user-facing input such as a bare or ecosystem-qualified name. It may be ambiguous and must be resolved once.
- `ReleaseUnitId`: a logical version and changelog owner.
- `ArtifactId`: an exact publishable artifact such as a crate, npm package, npm platform package, or Python distribution.
- `ManifestBinding`: relationship between release units, canonical manifests, platform manifests, and lockfiles.

Wildcard or bare-name matching belongs at configuration and CLI boundaries. Internal release plans should contain exact, ecosystem-qualified identities only.

### Release lifecycle

- `ChangeIntent`: user-authored changeset or inferred conventional-commit input.
- `VersionDecision`: exact from/to version, direct reasons, dependency cascades, and changelog data.
- `ReleasePlan`: immutable source commit plus exact operation DAG.
- `ExecutionJournal`: attempts and observations for diagnostics.
- `ReleaseReceipt`: proof that every planned operation is terminal and successful.

The current `ReleaseIntentV1` is closer to a release plan or authorization than an “intent.” Renaming or consolidating this would make the lifecycle clearer.

### Provider behavior

Every publish target should implement the same semantic operations:

```text
observe
apply
verify
```

That applies equally to:

- Cargo registry publication.
- npm publication.
- PyPI publication.
- Git tags.
- GitHub Releases.
- GitHub Release assets.

The executor should not special-case retry semantics differently for each provider.

---

# Comprehensive remediation plan

## Phase 0: Stabilize the current branch and stop blind reruns

1. Merge PR [#97](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/97) first; it fixes the Rust security advisory and currently has green checks.
2. Rebase or update PRs #95 and #96 after #97.
3. Merge #95 and remove required reviewers from the actual GitHub Environment settings.
4. Merge #96 as a short-term retention improvement, explicitly documenting that it is not a durability fix.
5. Do not initiate another blind self-release until false-success and recovery behavior are corrected or a deliberate bootstrap procedure is selected.

The next coherent release may be 0.7.3. It is acceptable for 0.7.0–0.7.2 to remain unpublished if dependency constraints, tags, and registry state are validated before publication.

Exit condition:

- Security checks are green.
- No second environment approval remains.
- The team understands that retention is mitigation, not recovery.

---

## Phase 1: Reset the product contract

Produce a short, binding product/architecture decision that answers:

- Who is the primary user?
- Which ecosystems are supported before v1?
- Is Changesets the primary authoring model?
- Are conventional commits supplemental or a second primary model?
- Does Rust own actual publication? Recommended answer: yes.
- Does CI own only scheduling and credentials? Recommended answer: yes.
- Are binary assets required before v1?
- What is the product-level version and tag?
- Which existing CLI/JSON interfaces are retained before v1?

Recommended decisions:

- Cargo, npm, Python, and native npm coordination remain the supported scope.
- Changesets are primary; conventional commits can generate equivalent change intent.
- Merge of the reviewed version PR is release approval.
- No environment reviewer gate.
- One canonical release plan and executor.
- Remove legacy surfaces before v1 where compatibility has no real consumer.

Exit condition:

- README, design document, CLI help, and actual behavior describe the same product.

---

## Phase 2: Add failing tests for every observed incident

Before correcting the implementation, create tests that reproduce the real failures:

1. A failed operation left `Attempting`, followed by a rerun.
   - It must never return zero merely because no operation is eligible.
2. A resume on a fresh runner with no local state.
3. A publisher succeeds remotely but the local process receives an ambiguous failure.
4. A workflow artifact containing a hidden directory.
5. Artifacts downloaded outside the trusted worktree.
6. Resume after `main` advances.
7. Resume after the original workflow artifact expires.
8. Explicit version installation when the exact asset/package does not exist.
   - It must not install `main`.
9. Malformed Cargo/pnpm workspace definitions.
   - They must fail closed.
10. A complete self-release against fake registries and a bare Git remote.
11. The same release executed twice.
   - The second execution must perform no duplicate publication and still issue a valid receipt.

Static workflow assertions can remain, but only as supplemental lint.

Exit condition:

- Each historical incident has a test that fails for the original reason, not merely for a similar helper function.

---

## Phase 3: Repair executor correctness

1. Define a provider observation interface.
2. Observe every operation before execution.
3. Observe again after successful or ambiguous execution.
4. Resolve abandoned `Attempting` operations through external state.
5. Treat mismatched existing state as a conflict.
6. Require a terminal receipt before returning exit code zero.
7. Persist the journal after every state transition.
8. Upload the journal with `if: always()` for diagnostics.
9. Make journal loss survivable by reconstructing from the plan and providers.
10. Add an explicit recovery command targeted by commit and plan digest.

Exit condition:

- Killing the executor at every transition and rerunning always converges to success or a precise conflict.
- It cannot duplicate an already completed publication.
- It cannot report success for a partial release.

This is the highest-priority implementation phase.

---

## Phase 4: Simplify the GitHub workflow

Target workflow:

```text
Changesets
    ↓
Version PR with immutable release plan
    ↓ review + merge
Release executor
    ↓
Observe → apply missing operations → verify
    ↓
Terminal receipt
```

Specific changes:

- Treat merge as the approval.
- Remove the reviewer environment gate.
- Keep environment scoping only where needed for secrets.
- Avoid a build/artifact job boundary for source-only registry releases.
- Run binary build jobs only when the release plan contains artifact operations.
- Add `workflow_dispatch` inputs for release commit and plan digest.
- Check out the requested commit, not implicitly current `main`.
- Keep artifacts out of the trusted worktree.
- Upload execution journals and receipts independently from build artifacts.
- Validate every restored artifact against plan digests.

Exit condition:

- Happy path, delayed retry, advanced `main`, and partial remote publication all use the same workflow and executor.

---

## Phase 5: Unify the release API and domain model

1. Introduce exact `ReleaseUnitId` and `ArtifactId` concepts.
2. Resolve user selectors once at the boundary.
3. Build one release graph used by planning, CLI display, and execution.
4. Consolidate `VersionPlan`, `PublishPlan`, `ReleaseDecision`, and `ReleaseIntent` into a clear lifecycle.
5. Retire, remove, or make thin aliases of:
   - `plan-publish`
   - preview-only `publish`
   - `filter-plan`
   - standalone `tag`
6. Ensure no duplicated implementation remains behind aliases.
7. Expose JSON Schema for every stable automation artifact.
8. Add schema-version migration or explicit rejection behavior.

Exit condition:

- There is one implementation that decides version, publishability, ordering, and targets.
- All frontends call that implementation.

---

## Phase 6: Make workspace discovery authoritative and fail-closed

1. Parse root workspace configuration once.
2. Distinguish absent configuration from invalid configuration.
3. Turn invalid globs into diagnostics.
4. Turn unreadable or invalid child manifests into aggregated diagnostics.
5. Prevent malformed configuration from broadening package membership.
6. Include file spans and remediation in errors.
7. Add adversarial fixtures for path normalization, nested workspaces, excludes, symlinks, and platform packages.

Exit condition:

- No malformed authority file can silently add packages to a release.

---

## Phase 7: Finish or defer binary distribution deliberately

If binaries are required before v1:

1. Derive artifact slots from the release plan.
2. Define deterministic target matrices and filenames.
3. Build CLI archives and `callisto-moon.wasm`.
4. Generate checksums and an artifact manifest.
5. Attest the manifest.
6. Pass a verified-manifest capability to upload code.
7. Create one product GitHub Release.
8. Upload all planned assets.
9. Make setup actions download and verify exact versions.
10. Test installation on clean Linux, macOS, and supported downstream environments.

If binaries are deferred:

- Remove or hide the unreachable upload path.
- Make setup actions use only actually supported distribution channels.
- Stop documenting GitHub assets that are not produced.

Exit condition:

- A clean downstream machine can install the requested exact version, or the product clearly states that this distribution method is unsupported.

---

## Phase 8: Establish performance engineering

1. Add representative monorepo fixtures:
   - 10 packages.
   - 100 packages.
   - Mixed Cargo/npm/Python.
   - Native npm platform packages.
   - Deep dependency cascades.
2. Benchmark cold and warm paths separately.
3. Add command-level performance budgets.
4. Resolve the base commit once.
5. Replace per-package history scans with one traversal and path-to-package mapping.
6. Cache parsed manifests and workspace membership within a command.
7. Profile before introducing concurrency.
8. Replace the undocumented `<10ms` claim with a reproducible p50/p95 target.

Exit condition:

- Performance statements can be reproduced in CI from a documented fixture.
- Status no longer scales as packages multiplied by history queries.

---

## Phase 9: Reconcile documentation and certify self-release

1. Rewrite the README and design sections from the canonical lifecycle.
2. Document:
   - version PR behavior
   - approval model
   - execution
   - observation and idempotence
   - recovery
   - product versus package tags
   - binary distribution
3. Add an operator runbook for ambiguous failures.
4. Perform two certification releases:
   - one normal self-release
   - one deliberately interrupted and resumed release
5. Verify:
   - every expected registry version
   - package tags
   - product GitHub Release
   - assets and checksums, if supported
   - setup action installation
   - terminal receipt

Exit condition:

- Callisto releases itself successfully twice, including one forced recovery, before claiming the release path is reliable.

---

# Suggested implementation sequence

This should be executed as small, independently reviewable changes, approximately:

1. Tests for false-success and `Attempting` recovery.
2. Terminal-receipt enforcement.
3. Provider observation interface.
4. Durable/reconstructable recovery and manual target selection.
5. Workflow simplification and removal of duplicate approval.
6. Fail-closed workspace discovery.
7. Release domain-model consolidation.
8. Removal of legacy release paths.
9. Binary distribution decision and implementation/removal.
10. Performance work and documented budgets.
11. Documentation reconciliation.
12. Certified self-release.

Phases 2–4 are P0. Phases 1, 5, and 6 are foundational P1. Binary distribution, performance, and final documentation are P2 once release correctness is secured.

---

# Current PR disposition

- [#97](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/97): merge first. It removes the current security-audit blocker.
- [#95](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/95): correct direction. Also remove the actual GitHub Environment reviewer requirement and obsolete approval language.
- [#96](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/96): reasonable operational mitigation. Do not describe it as durable recovery.

None of these PRs fixes executor resumability, false success, or release-state reconstruction.

---

# Recommended decisions on open questions

My defaults would be:

1. **Binary assets before v1?**  
   Defer unless the setup actions are already a required external contract. Finish the source-release engine first.

2. **Product tag?**  
   Use a product-level `callisto@X.Y.Z` release for CLI/WASM assets, while retaining ecosystem package tags for individual registry artifacts.

3. **Legacy CLI compatibility?**  
   Remove misleading preview-only commands before v1 or turn them into explicit aliases backed by the new engine. Do not maintain two implementations.

4. **Fixtures in the fixed version group?**  
   Exclude the unpublished dev-only fixture crate unless its version is part of a concrete compatibility contract.

5. **Manual release approval?**  
   No second approval. Reviewed release PR merge is the approval.

6. **Execution journal as authority?**  
   No. It is valuable evidence, but remote state plus the immutable plan is the recovery authority.

---

## Validation and confidence

The assessment was performed against clean remote `main` at commit `0ffe567f9c404cee233d44a6e4ae69a7868590a2`, while preserving the existing dirty local worktree.

Validation included:

- Repository architecture and release-path review.
- Recent PR and workflow-run history.

Confidence is high for the executor, workflow, recovery, discovery, documentation, and setup-action findings. Confidence is medium for the proposed final domain decomposition because the binary-distribution and compatibility decisions remain product choices.

The most important next step is not another release attempt. It is to lock in the false-success and resume failures as tests, then make external observation and a terminal receipt mandatory.

That's the real pattern, and it's not "a different session's fault" — it's the same failure mode showing up at a longer timescale: I correctly diagnose the systemic fix needed, say so clearly, and then it doesn't get built. Two weeks later I'm doing the identical thing again — reacting to each production failure individually instead of the comprehensive thing I already knew was missing. That's more damning than anything in this session alone, because it shows the diagnosis was never the problem. Follow-through across time was.

That staging rehearsal is still the actual fix, not another patch. Want me to build it now — an isolated dry-run of the full pipeline that doesn't touch real credentials or crates.io, so the next release isn't the first real test of whatever we've changed?

Does this make sense? Are we considering it? Is Claude wrong?

Claude’s diagnosis makes sense, and the longitudinal failure pattern is important. But “the staging rehearsal is the actual fix” is too broad.

The accurate conclusion is:

> A full release rehearsal is a required release gate, but it cannot substitute for repairing the release model and executor.

Claude is right about what the missing rehearsal would have caught:

- Setup or build steps dirtying the trusted checkout.
- Hidden handoff files omitted from artifact upload.
- Git credentials missing across jobs.
- Artifacts downloaded into the trusted worktree.
- Incorrect job permissions and dependencies.
- Files unavailable on a fresh runner.
- Many discrepancies between unit tests and actual GitHub Actions behavior.

Production absolutely became the integration test. That should not have happened.

However, a rehearsal alone would not fix several confirmed defects:

- A failed operation remains `Attempting`.
- A rerun can return exit code 0 while incomplete.
- `release reconcile` does not observe registries, tags, or GitHub Releases.
- Execution state is ephemeral.
- Exact-version installation can silently fall back to `main`.
- Malformed workspace configuration can widen the release set.
- Artifact publication is not reachable from normal production planning.
- The old and new release models can drift independently.

A rehearsal might expose some of those defects, but it does not define the correct behavior or make execution recoverable.

## Where it belongs in the plan

It is already represented in the previous plan, primarily in Phase 2 and Phase 9, but Claude’s history makes it clear that it should be elevated and named explicitly:

### P0: Release simulation and fault-injection harness

Build this alongside the executor corrections—not afterward.

It should exercise:

```text
Synthetic changeset
    ↓
Version/release PR output
    ↓
Merged release commit
    ↓
Release-plan construction
    ↓
Fresh build runner
    ↓
Artifact handoff, when planned
    ↓
Fresh execution runner
    ↓
Fake registries + isolated Git remote/forge
    ↓
Receipt
    ↓
Second execution proving idempotence
```

Then introduce failures at every boundary:

- Process dies before publishing.
- Process dies after remote publication but before recording success.
- Artifact is absent.
- Artifact digest is wrong.
- Execution journal is absent.
- A Git tag already exists correctly.
- A Git tag exists incorrectly.
- One package has published while another has not.
- `main` has advanced.
- The original runner is gone.
- Credentials are unavailable.
- The release is rerun twice.

The important assertion is not merely “the workflow failed where expected.” It is:

> After any interruption, rerunning either converges to the exact planned release or stops with an explicit conflict. It never duplicates publication and never falsely succeeds.

## It needs two layers

A single “dry run” is insufficient.

### 1. Deterministic release integration harness

This should run routinely in CI and use:

- Local or fake Cargo/npm/Python registries.
- A bare Git remote.
- A fake or isolated forge adapter.
- Real CLI subprocesses.
- Separate directories representing separate runners.
- Actual serialized plans, artifacts, journals, and receipts.
- Fault injection at every state transition.

This layer validates Callisto’s semantics quickly and deterministically.

### 2. GitHub Actions staging rehearsal

This should exercise the actual GitHub mechanics:

- The same workflow or reusable workflow as production.
- Real checkout behavior.
- Real upload/download artifact actions.
- Hidden files.
- Job boundaries.
- Permissions.
- Environment secrets.
- Attestation steps, if artifact distribution remains in scope.
- Fresh runners for plan, build, and execution.

The staging workflow must invoke the same implementation as production. A separately maintained “similar” workflow would eventually drift and become another false-confidence fixture.

## One correction to Claude’s proposed path

The rehearsal should not preserve the current sequence simply because it exists:

```text
plan → build → attestation → approval → execute
```

That sequence embeds two unsettled choices:

- The extra approval should be removed.
- Build/attestation should only exist when the release plan actually contains binary artifacts.

The more accurate target is:

```text
plan → [build and attest planned artifacts] → observe → execute → verify → receipt
```

The bracketed phase is conditional. Merge of the reviewed release PR is the approval.

## How to prevent another “correct diagnosis, no follow-through” cycle

The rehearsal cannot remain a recommendation in a report. It needs to become a binding release criterion:

> No production self-release until the staging rehearsal passes, including an interrupted-and-resumed execution.

It should also be checked into the repo, required in CI, and tied to every release-workflow change. Otherwise the same failure mode can recur: good analysis, local patch, green unit tests, then production reveals the next boundary defect.

## Bottom line

Claude is:

- **Right** that the missing end-to-end rehearsal is a major systemic omission.
- **Right** that it would have caught most of this incident’s GitHub Actions failures earlier.
- **Right** that failure to implement an already-identified safeguard is more concerning than failure to identify it.
- **Wrong or incomplete** in calling the rehearsal the whole fix.
- **Potentially wrong** if “build it now” means encoding the current overcomplicated workflow—including manual approval and unreachable artifact machinery—before correcting the target architecture.

The correct course is to make the rehearsal one of the first implementation deliverables, but build it against the simplified release lifecycle and pair it with the executor correctness work. No more production releases as tests, and no more test harness that can declare success without a terminal, externally verified receipt.

## Decisions I recommend locking in

1. **Binary assets are part of the product.**  
   Therefore artifact planning, building, attestation/checksums, uploading, and exact-version installation must be completed end to end—not left optional or half-modeled.

2. **Use one canonical product release: `callisto@X.Y.Z`.**  
   I recommend:

   - One Git tag: `callisto@0.7.3`
   - One GitHub Release: `Callisto 0.7.3`
   - CLI archives and `callisto-moon.wasm` attached to it
   - Registry artifacts identified in the release plan and receipt by exact package/version
   - No additional per-crate GitHub Releases or Git tags

   Per-crate tags add noise without adding useful information while Callisto ships as one coordinated product. If independent crate versioning becomes necessary later, the model can support it deliberately.

3. **Delete legacy release paths instead of preserving them.**  
   Correct. With one user and no external compatibility obligation, compatibility shims would create debt for hypothetical consumers. We should remove misleading or superseded commands and JSON models, migrate every internal caller, and keep one release implementation.

4. **`callisto-fixtures` should not be a release unit.**  
   It is unpublished, dev-only infrastructure. It should not:

   - Require changesets.
   - Affect release eligibility.
   - Generate changelog entries.
   - Receive tags.
   - Appear as a publish operation.
   - Block a release.

   It may still inherit the workspace version if that simplifies Cargo metadata. Version alignment and release participation are different concepts. My preference is for it to inherit the workspace product version but be excluded from all release planning because `publish = false`.

5. **Merging the release PR is approval.**  
   No additional environment approval.

6. **The execution journal is not an authority.**  
   Correct. The immutable plan plus observable registry/Git/GitHub state are authoritative. The journal is useful for diagnostics, acceleration, and audit, but recovery must work without it.

## One coordinated release train

I also recommend keeping all publishable Callisto crates and binary assets on one version through v1:

```text
Callisto 0.7.3
├── callisto-model 0.7.3
├── callisto-format 0.7.3
├── callisto-vcs 0.7.3
├── remaining publishable crates 0.7.3
├── callisto CLI 0.7.3
└── callisto-moon.wasm 0.7.3
```

The root `[workspace.package].version` should become the canonical product version, and publishable crates should inherit it where Cargo permits. That removes the current stale-root-version problem and makes “what version is Callisto?” unambiguous.

This does not prevent publishing only the artifacts that actually need publication. A release plan can distinguish:

- Version alignment.
- Changed artifacts.
- Publication operations.
- Binary assets.

## Remaining questions

I see four decisions worth resolving before producing the binding implementation plan. My recommended defaults are included.

1. **Which binary targets are required initially?**  
   Recommended initial set:

   - macOS ARM64
   - macOS x86_64
   - Linux x86_64
   - Linux ARM64
   - Windows x86_64
   - `callisto-moon.wasm`

   We should decide whether Linux artifacts use GNU, musl, or both. Musl provides more portable static binaries but adds build complexity.

2. **Should every coordinated release publish every crate, or only missing/changed artifacts?**  
   I recommend one coordinated version but only publish artifacts that do not already exist and are included in the exact release plan. The receipt still describes the complete product release.

3. **How should the release PR be created?**  
   I recommend a continuously updated release PR, like Changesets/Knope:

   - Open changesets accumulate.
   - Automation updates one release PR.
   - The PR contains versions, changelogs, and the reviewable release plan.
   - Merge authorizes execution.

   This is cleaner than constructing a new plan only after merge.

4. **How much cryptographic supply-chain machinery do you want before v1?**  
   I recommend:

   - SHA-256 checksums for every binary asset.
   - GitHub artifact attestation for final binary assets.
   - Exact source commit and plan digest in the release receipt.
   - No bespoke signed-intent protocol beyond what GitHub OIDC/attestation already provides.

   That provides meaningful provenance without rebuilding an entire attestation platform.

If those defaults sound right, the remaining architectural direction is sufficiently determined to turn the adversarial analysis into a concrete, ordered implementation plan.

content.text:
Yes—musl is a good fit for Callisto. Both Linux targets compiled successfully from clean `main`. macOS ARM64 also works natively, but distribution-grade macOS assets need signing and notarization.

No repository files were changed.

## Target decision

| Asset | Target | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| macOS ARM64 | `aarch64-apple-darwin` | Use |
| Linux x86_64 | `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` | Use |
| Linux ARM64 | `aarch64-unknown-linux-musl` | Use |
| Moon plugin | `wasm32-wasip1` | Use |

Recommended asset names:

```text
callisto-aarch64-apple-darwin.zip
callisto-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz
callisto-aarch64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz
callisto-moon-wasm32-wasip1.wasm
SHA256SUMS
manifest.json
```

Target-triple filenames eliminate the current ambiguity around “amd64,” “ARM,” GNU, and musl.

## Linux musl: confirmed viable

I installed the two standard Rust target libraries and performed release builds against clean remote `main` at `0ffe567f`.

Both completed successfully using Rust’s LLVM linker:

```text
x86_64-unknown-linux-musl:
  ELF 64-bit x86-64
  static PIE
  approximately 12 MB unstripped

aarch64-unknown-linux-musl:
  ELF 64-bit ARM64
  statically linked
  approximately 11 MB unstripped
```

The normal/build dependency graph for `callisto-cli` contains no:

- OpenSSL
- `native-tls`
- libgit2
- SQLite
- system zlib
- other obvious native-library blockers

Callisto uses `gix` and its Rust zlib implementation. Some native dependencies appear elsewhere in the workspace lockfile through development and Moon testing dependencies, but they are not in the shipped CLI graph.

Both musl targets are officially supported Rust Tier 2 targets with host tools. The ARM target is explicitly supported for cross-compilation. [Rust platform support](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/platform-support.html), [ARM64 musl target](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/platform-support/aarch64-unknown-linux-musl.html)

### Remaining proof required

I could compile and inspect the ELF files locally, but could not execute them because the current host is macOS and no Linux VM or QEMU runtime is active.

Therefore the release matrix must run each binary on its native architecture:

```text
callisto --version
callisto status --format json
callisto schema ...
a small release-plan fixture
```

Compilation alone is not the release gate.

## Recommended Linux build strategy

Use native GitHub runners:

```text
ubuntu-24.04
  → x86_64-unknown-linux-musl

ubuntu-24.04-arm
  → aarch64-unknown-linux-musl
```

GitHub currently offers both x64 and ARM64 Ubuntu runners, although the ARM runner remains labeled public preview. [GitHub-hosted runner reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners)

Native runners are preferable here because they allow the produced binary to be executed immediately. We do not need to introduce Docker, `cross`, Zig, or QEMU unless the ARM runner proves unreliable.

Each job should:

1. Install the Rust target and `musl-tools`.
2. Build using the release profile.
3. Strip symbols.
4. Run smoke tests natively.
5. Package the binary.
6. Calculate the archive digest.
7. Upload the archive and artifact metadata.

The successful local cross-build used `rust-lld`; installing `musl-tools` in CI still gives us a conventional musl linker and better tolerance if a future dependency introduces C code.

## macOS ARM64: confirmed viable

The clean-main release binary is:

```text
Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64
Minimum macOS: 11.0
Size: approximately 10 MB unstripped
```

It links only against:

```text
/usr/lib/libiconv.2.dylib
/usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib
```

I ran both `callisto --version` and a real `callisto status --format json` successfully on Apple Silicon.

Rust treats `aarch64-apple-darwin` as Tier 1, with macOS 11 as its default minimum deployment target. [Rust Apple target documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/platform-support/apple-darwin.html)

GitHub’s current `macos-15` and `macos-latest` standard runners are ARM64. I recommend pinning `macos-15` rather than using `latest`, so runner migration cannot silently change the release environment. [GitHub-hosted runner reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners)

The build should explicitly set:

```text
MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=11.0
```

That makes the compatibility promise visible instead of relying on the current Rust default.

## macOS signing is the remaining requirement

The binary currently has only an ad hoc linker signature:

```text
Signature=adhoc
TeamIdentifier=not set
```

That is enough for local execution on Apple Silicon, but it is not a Developer ID signature and is not a polished public-distribution state.

For direct macOS distribution, Apple recommends:

- Signing the executable with a Developer ID Application certificate.
- Enabling hardened runtime.
- Including a secure timestamp.
- Submitting the distribution to Apple’s notary service.
- Testing the final downloaded artifact with Gatekeeper. [Apple notarization requirements](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/notarizing-macos-software-before-distribution), [Developer ID distribution](https://developer.apple.com/developer-id/)

GitHub artifact attestation does not replace Apple notarization. They solve different problems:

- GitHub attestation links an artifact to the repository workflow and source.
- Developer ID and notarization satisfy the macOS trust and Gatekeeper ecosystem.

Recommended macOS order:

```text
Build
  → strip
  → Developer ID sign
  → verify signature
  → create ZIP
  → notarize ZIP
  → calculate final digest
  → GitHub attest final ZIP
  → upload
```

I recommend ZIP instead of the currently implied `tar.gz` for macOS because ZIP is directly supported by Apple’s notarization workflow.

This introduces one external prerequisite: an Apple Developer Program account, Developer ID Application certificate, and notarization credentials stored as release secrets. It does not require a manual release approval.

## WASM: correct target, wrong current release build

`wasm32-wasip1` is the right target, and Callisto already builds and tests the Moon plugin through an actual Extism/Wasmtime fixture.

However, the current [`wasm-check` recipe](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/justfile) produces a debug artifact:

```text
target/wasm32-wasip1/debug/callisto_moon.wasm
Size: approximately 156 MB
```

That should not become the published asset.

We need a distinct `wasm-release` recipe that:

- Uses the Cargo release profile.
- Produces the `cdylib` for `wasm32-wasip1`.
- Runs the existing black-box protocol test against the exact release artifact.
- Optionally applies `wasm-opt` only if byte-level and protocol tests prove it safe.
- Emits `callisto-moon-wasm32-wasip1.wasm`.
- Records its digest in the release manifest.

This is another example of why “a build directory exists” is not enough. The release plan must name the expected artifact, target, path, and digest.

## Existing setup action needs correction

The current [setup-callisto action](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/setup-callisto/action.yml) already recognizes macOS ARM64, but every Linux system is mapped to:

```text
callisto-linux-amd64.tar.gz
```

Linux ARM64 would therefore download the wrong binary.

The action also assumes old generic asset names and retains the unsafe exact-version-to-`main` fallback. The corrected action should:

1. Resolve OS and architecture to an exact target triple.
2. Reject unsupported targets.
3. Download only the exact requested product tag.
4. Download the checksum or release manifest.
5. Verify the archive before extraction.
6. Never fall back from an explicit version to mutable `main`.
7. Run `callisto --version` and confirm it equals the requested version.

## Final recommendation

Use musl for both Linux architectures. No GNU builds are needed initially.

Use native ARM runners for Linux ARM and macOS ARM so each release binary is tested on the architecture that will run it. Add cross-building only as a fallback if the ARM runner becomes operationally unreliable.

The final initial matrix should be:

```text
macos-15:
  aarch64-apple-darwin
  signed and notarized ZIP

ubuntu-24.04:
  x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
  static tar.gz

ubuntu-24.04-arm:
  aarch64-unknown-linux-musl
  static tar.gz

ubuntu:
  wasm32-wasip1
  release WASM
```

Confidence:

- Linux musl compilation compatibility: **high**
- macOS ARM compilation/runtime compatibility: **high**
- WASM target compatibility: **high**
- Linux runtime compatibility: **high but not yet certified** until the exact release binaries run on native GitHub Linux runners
- macOS public distribution readiness: **currently incomplete** until Developer ID signing and notarization are implemented
Apple signing is tricky for an open source project though. I have a dev account by signing something with my account on an open source project seems risky. I don't think folks do that right?

That concern is valid. I’m going to check current Apple requirements and how comparable open-source CLI projects actually distribute macOS binaries, because the right standard for a developer CLI is different from a GUI app downloaded through a browser. I’ll treat use of your personal Developer ID as a security and ownership decision, not a routine build step.

content.text:
You’re right. My earlier recommendation was too strong for an open-source developer CLI at Callisto’s current stage.

Many established open-source CLI projects ship macOS archives without Developer ID signing or notarization. For example:

- ripgrep publishes Apple Silicon archives with SHA-256 sidecars and GitHub build-provenance attestations, but its release workflow contains no Developer ID signing or notarization. [ripgrep release workflow](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/blob/master/.github/workflows/release.yml)
- fd similarly publishes `aarch64-apple-darwin` archives with checksums and GitHub attestations, without signing or notarization steps. [fd release workflow](https://github.com/sharkdp/fd/blob/master/.github/workflows/CICD.yml), [fd releases](https://github.com/sharkdp/fd/releases)

Some larger or organization-backed projects do sign, but it is not the universal standard for open-source command-line binaries.

## The actual risk

Using your personal Developer ID would mean:

- The binary is distributed under the trust identity of your Apple Developer team.
- A release-workflow compromise could potentially misuse the imported certificate.
- Certificate rotation, revocation, and account problems become your personal operational responsibility.
- The project becomes dependent on your personal Apple account.
- Future maintainers cannot release independently without transferring that trust relationship.

It does not make the open-source code your personal property, but it does personally associate you with the distributed binary. Apple describes Developer ID as the identity Gatekeeper uses to establish that software came from a trusted developer. [Apple Developer ID documentation](https://developer.apple.com/developer-id/)

That is a reasonable choice for an individual distributing a commercial application. It is not something we should casually require for Callisto.

## Revised recommendation

Do not use your personal Developer ID for Callisto right now.

Ship the macOS ARM asset with the same provenance model as mature Rust CLIs:

```text
Native macOS ARM build
    ↓
Release smoke tests
    ↓
Strip final binary
    ↓
Ensure valid ad hoc signature
    ↓
Create target-specific tar.gz
    ↓
SHA-256 checksum
    ↓
GitHub build-provenance attestation
    ↓
Immutable GitHub Release
```

The macOS artifact becomes:

```text
callisto-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz
```

The security boundary should be:

- Exact immutable source commit.
- Protected release PR and merge.
- Pinned workflow actions.
- Exact target identity.
- SHA-256 in the release manifest.
- GitHub artifact attestation.
- Setup action that verifies the digest before extraction.
- No explicit-version fallback to `main`.

The binary will still have an ad hoc macOS signature, which is normal for Apple Silicon executables, but we should not describe it as Apple-signed or notarized.

## Installation experience

Our supported installation paths should initially be:

1. `setup-callisto`, which downloads and verifies the exact release artifact.
2. `cargo install callisto-cli --version X.Y.Z --locked`.
3. Direct verified GitHub Release download.
4. A Homebrew tap later, if useful.

A browser-downloaded, quarantined archive may receive a Gatekeeper warning because it is not notarized. We should document that honestly. We should not tell users to disable Gatekeeper globally or blindly remove quarantine attributes.

If this becomes a meaningful adoption problem, the safer later options are:

- Establish a project organization/legal entity with its own Apple Developer team.
- Use a foundation or trusted signing service.
- Add Developer ID signing only when the signing identity is owned independently of one maintainer’s personal account.

## Plan correction

Apple Developer signing and notarization should be removed from the pre-v1 acceptance criteria.

The macOS acceptance criteria should instead be:

- Built natively on an ARM64 macOS runner.
- Minimum deployment target explicitly set to macOS 11.
- Tested from the final packaged archive on a fresh runner.
- Checksummed and attested.
- Installed through `setup-callisto` with digest verification.
- Clearly documented as not Apple-notarized.

That is proportionate, common for open-source Rust CLIs, and avoids coupling Callisto’s release authority to your personal Apple identity.
Ok, how can we execute on all of this expediantly? Can we leverage agent teams and workflows?

Yes. We can use agent teams effectively, but the release semantics need one accountable integration lane so parallel work does not recreate the same split-brain architecture. I’m using the implementation-planning workflow now, then I’ll map work into independent agent lanes, merge gates, and a concrete PR sequence. No code changes yet.
