content.text:
Yes. Agent teams can accelerate this substantially, provided we stabilize the semantic contract first and give every agent exclusive file ownership. Starting several agents against the current ambiguous release model would generate competing fixes.

## Recommended delivery workflow

```text
Persisted release specification
        ↓
Adversarial spec gate
        ↓
Dependency-ordered implementation plan
        ↓
Agent implementation waves
        ↓
Independent verification
        ↓
Changeset + reviewed PR
        ↓
Full staging rehearsal
        ↓
Merge release PR = production approval
```

The decisions currently exist only in this conversation. The first expedient step is making them durable so an agent cannot “rediscover” or reinterpret the architecture halfway through implementation.

## Step 1: Lock the contract

Create one binding release specification covering:

- One coordinated product version.
- Canonical `callisto@X.Y.Z` tag and GitHub Release.
- Continuously updated release PR.
- Merging that PR is the only human approval.
- No environment reviewer gate.
- Exact source commit and plan digest.
- Exact ecosystem-qualified artifact identities.
- `Absent`, `AlreadyPresent`, `Unverifiable`, and `Conflict` observations.
- A terminal receipt required for exit code zero.
- Recovery without an execution journal.
- Manual resume by commit and plan digest.
- macOS ARM64, Linux x86_64 musl, Linux ARM64 musl, and WASI assets.
- Checksums and GitHub attestations.
- No personal Apple Developer signing.
- `callisto-fixtures` excluded from release participation.
- One release engine; superseded paths are removed.
- Full staging rehearsal required before production.

Then run it through an adversarial spec review before implementation. This should catch contradictory criteria before they become code.

## Step 2: Use one coordinator and three bounded lanes

All agents share the workspace, so ownership must be explicit.

| Lane | Ownership | Must not edit |
|---|---|---|
| Coordinator | Shared release types, provider contract, task ordering, production workflow, final integration | Nothing delegated without coordination |
| Executor agent | Release execution, observation, recovery, receipt enforcement, CLI exit behavior | GitHub workflows and packaging scripts |
| Rehearsal agent | Integration fixtures, fault injection, fresh-runner tests, staging workflow tests | Core semantic types and production workflow |
| Distribution agent | Native/WASM builders, packaging, manifest generation, checksums, setup action | Executor and registry providers |

Initial ownership would look approximately like this:

### Coordinator

- `callisto-model` release contracts.
- Stable JSON schemas.
- Removal/migration of superseded release models.
- Provider trait/interface.
- `.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml`.
- Final cross-lane integration.

### Executor agent

- [release_execution.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_execution.rs)
- [release_store.rs](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_store.rs)
- [release CLI command](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release.rs)
- Registry, Git, and forge observer implementations.
- Terminal receipt and exit-code tests.

### Rehearsal agent

- New release fixture workspace.
- Fake/local registry adapters.
- Bare Git remote and forge fixture.
- Kill-point and ambiguous-failure tests.
- Fresh-directory/fresh-runner execution tests.
- GitHub workflow contract tests.

### Distribution agent

- Native target matrix.
- Release WASM recipe.
- Artifact manifest generation.
- Packaging and stripping.
- Checksums and attestable inputs.
- [setup-callisto action](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/setup-callisto/action.yml).
- Exact-version installation tests.

Agents should work in parallel only after the coordinator lands the shared contract. That prevents everyone from inventing a different interpretation of `AlreadyPresent`, artifact identity, or completion.

## Step 3: Deliver in implementation waves

### Wave 0: Current operational cleanup

Before architectural implementation:

- Land the security advisory fix.
- Remove the workflow environment-review check.
- Remove the required reviewer from the actual GitHub Environment.
- Treat longer artifact retention as mitigation only.
- Do not merge the release PR until certification.

Normal feature PRs may continue to accumulate changesets. The continuously updated release PR remains unmerged, so no production release is authorized.

### Wave 1: Canonical semantic cutover

This is primarily coordinator-owned and should be serial.

Deliver:

- `PackageSelector`
- `ReleaseUnitId`
- `ArtifactId`
- `VersionDecision`
- `ReleasePlan`
- `Operation`
- `Observation`
- `ExecutionJournal`
- `ReleaseReceipt`

Migrate every caller and delete superseded models and commands in the same change. Because there is no compatibility obligation, we should not leave aliases or parallel implementations behind.

Gate:

```text
just fmt-check
just lint
just test
just wasm-check
```

Every stable JSON artifact must have an exposed schema and fixture.

### Wave 2: Three parallel implementation lanes

Once the interfaces compile:

```text
                    ┌─ Executor and provider observation
Canonical contract ─┼─ Failure/recovery rehearsal harness
                    └─ Binary and WASM artifact builders
```

#### Executor outcome

- An `Attempting` operation is always observed on resume.
- Matching remote state becomes `AlreadyPresent`.
- Conflicting or unverifiable state fails loudly.
- No eligible operation does not imply completion.
- Exit zero requires a valid terminal receipt.
- Journal loss is survivable.
- Manual resume accepts and validates a commit plus plan digest.

#### Rehearsal outcome

The harness interrupts execution at every transition:

- Before publication.
- After publication but before recording success.
- Between dependent packages.
- Before tag creation.
- Before GitHub Release creation.
- Before and after asset upload.
- With missing, expired, or corrupted artifacts.
- With `main` advanced.
- With the journal deleted.

Every rerun must converge or report a precise conflict.

#### Distribution outcome

Produce and test:

```text
callisto-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz
callisto-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz
callisto-aarch64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz
callisto-moon-wasm32-wasip1.wasm
SHA256SUMS
manifest.json
```

Each native job runs the final packaged binary before upload. The setup action downloads an exact tag, verifies the manifest and checksum, and refuses to fall back to `main`.

### Wave 3: Workflow integration

The coordinator integrates all three lanes into one release workflow:

```text
Version PR
    ↓ merge
Load immutable plan
    ↓
Build only planned binary assets
    ↓
Verify plan and artifact digests
    ↓
Observe registry/Git/GitHub state
    ↓
Apply missing operations
    ↓
Verify every operation
    ↓
Create terminal receipt
```

Properties:

- No approval job.
- No transient state as correctness authority.
- Build jobs only when the plan includes binary assets.
- Execution artifacts kept outside the trusted checkout.
- Journals and receipts uploaded with `if: always()`.
- Manual dispatch accepts an immutable release target.
- Every restored artifact is digest-verified.

### Wave 4: Full staging rehearsal

Use two complementary layers.

#### Deterministic CI harness

Runs for every change affecting release behavior:

- Local Cargo/npm/Python registry fixtures.
- Bare Git remote.
- Fake forge boundary.
- Separate directories for every simulated runner.
- Real CLI subprocesses and serialized artifacts.
- Fault injection.

#### GitHub Actions staging repository

Use an isolated repository to exercise actual GitHub behavior:

- The same reusable workflow as production.
- Real `upload-artifact` and `download-artifact`.
- Real job permissions.
- Real Git tag and GitHub Release creation.
- Synthetic package names and test registry endpoints.
- No Callisto production credentials.

The production and staging workflows must call the same reusable workflow. A copied “staging-like” YAML file would drift.

Creating the staging repository and its credentials is an external operation, so I would request your approval immediately before doing it.

### Wave 5: Product correctness cleanup

After the self-release path is safe, teams can work in parallel again:

- Fail-closed workspace discovery.
- Performance traversal and benchmark budgets.
- Removal of documentation contradictions.
- Root workspace-version normalization.
- Exclusion of fixtures from release participation.
- Setup and installation documentation.

These should finish before v1, but they need not block development of the executor and binary pipeline.

## PR structure

Avoid a mega-PR. I recommend these transactional review boundaries:

1. `docs: define canonical Callisto release lifecycle`
2. `refactor(release): replace parallel release models with canonical plan`
3. `test(release): add interrupted execution and recovery fixtures`
4. `fix(release): reconcile external state and require terminal receipt`
5. `feat(release): resume by source commit and plan digest`
6. `feat(dist): build and verify native and WASI assets`
7. `fix(setup): require exact verified release artifacts`
8. `ci(release): execute canonical plan through reusable workflow`
9. `test(release): add complete staging release rehearsal`
10. `fix(discovery): reject malformed workspace authority`
11. `perf(status): batch changed-package history traversal`
12. `docs: align product and recovery documentation`

Each PR gets:

- Its own changeset when consumer-facing.
- Targeted tests.
- `just ci`.
- An independent adversarial review.
- No remote push or PR creation until you confirm it.

## Independent verification

Do not let the implementing agent approve its own work.

After each wave, use a fresh adversarial agent to verify:

- Every interface implementation was migrated.
- No sibling release path remains.
- Failure behavior matches the spec.
- Tests fail for the original bug, not a synthetic approximation.
- No false-success path remains.
- No workflow job silently skipped its meaningful work.

Before the first production release, run a final lifecycle gate against the specification and require evidence for every acceptance criterion.

## What agent teams should not do

To stay fast, we should explicitly forbid:

- Multiple agents editing `callisto-model::release` simultaneously.
- One agent patching the workflow while another changes its JSON contract.
- Separate staging and production release implementations.
- Compatibility wrappers for removed pre-v1 behavior.
- Agents creating commits, pushes, PRs, releases, repositories, or credentials without confirmation.
- Declaring completion from unit tests without the full rehearsal.

## Immediate next action

There are no remaining product questions blocking the local work.

The next step should be to persist the release specification and its dependency-ordered implementation plan—without changing production code—then present both for your approval. Once approved, I can execute the first semantic cutover and launch the three bounded agent lanes against stable interfaces.
Does this plan leverage the latest version of our plugins?

### Agent-team orchestration moves into Smith

Smith 2.4.2 already supports:

- Bounded parallel implementation.

- Explicit file ownership.
- Risk-matched testing.
- Defect-family review.

We should let Navigator define the batches and Smith execute them using packaged role cards. I should remain the integration owner, but we do not need to invent a parallel orchestration protocol from scratch.

### The findings become durable Ranger evidence

The existing audit is currently prose in this conversation. Ranger should convert the confirmed defects into `finding-report@2`. That gives Scribe’s architecture workflow a typed input and prevents findings from disappearing during context compression.

We should not rerun the entire investigation. The existing evidence should be normalized into the current artifact contract.

### Structural correction goes through Scribe

The split release models, journal-as-authority problem, and duplicated semantic paths are architectural defects, not ordinary implementation tasks.

Scribe 3.3.2 should produce the structural correction, refresh the architecture model, and then draft and gate the behavioral specification.

### Navigator should produce actual execution batches

Navigator 2.3.2 supports:

- A hash of the approved specification.
- Criterion-to-task coverage.
- Exact file targets.
- Interface-implementation coverage.
- Dependency-aware batches.
- Drift detection if the specification changes.

That should replace the informal PR sequence I previously gave.

### Current schema versions matter

The implementation should use the current contracts:

- `requirement@1`
- `research-report@1`
- `finding-report@2`
- `spec@1`
- `plan@1`
- `implementation-review@2`

We should not produce older verdict or finding formats.

- **Mason** evaluates and authors plugins; it is not the correct tool for Callisto’s release rehearsal.

content.text: The reference-tool research is complete and it sharpens the design: Callisto should combine Nx’s fixed release group, Release Please’s merged-PR boundary, Changesets/Nx’s unpublished-version checks, and Knope’s draft-release asset staging—but strengthen all four with exact external read-back and fresh-runner convergence. None of those tools provides the full rehearsal or cross-registry completion proof we need, so copying one wholesale would reproduce the same confidence gap.

content.text: All five specifications now pass the independent adversarial and architecture reviews. The last blocker was subtle but important: public release metadata and its checksum originally depended on each other’s final digest. That cycle is removed—the metadata is built from validated payload entries first, then the checksum and final manifest close the set. I’m issuing the spec gates and persisting the passed contracts next; no production code or release action has been changed yet.

The independent PM-004 review found three serious gaps before they could become provider bugs: missing credential-source policy, validation that trusts a self-consistent forged decision, and a hard-coded generic Python wheel name. I’m correcting all three at the model/graph boundary rather than allowing dispatch to guess.

The decision issue has a clean fix already supported by the repository: validation will re-read the canonical decision from the exact release commit and compare it to the intent, instead of validating an intent against its own embedded data. The observer module is drafted with remote tag checks, supported GitHub API use, strict registry evidence, and cached provider snapshots.

The observer now type-checks cleanly; its only remaining project blocker is the intentionally unmigrated executor. Two PM-004 blockers are fixed: validation now independently reads the commit-authored decision at `.callisto/release-decision.json`, and GitHub HTTPS/SSH remotes canonicalize repository path case. The remaining PM-004 blocker is the explicit Python distribution descriptor API, which is actively being added rather than guessed.

The Python descriptor is using a strict `{version}` filename template, not a literal per-release name. That keeps wheel tags/platforms explicit while deterministically binding the release version into the immutable intent—no guessed filenames and no config edits on every release.

The dispatcher contract is now constrained to one observation session plus the validated artifact capability. It will not decide that a provider is “missing” on its own, and it will re-read the exact bytes immediately before an irreversible effect.

The direct Cargo publish body needs safe inspection of the validated `.crate` archive, so I authorized the planned bounded gzip/tar dependencies. The dispatcher will parse the verified buffer only—never rebuild from a mutable package directory or extract archive paths to disk.

+# Self-release lifecycle
+
+This document is the operational contract for Callisto's own releases. The implementation plan
+is [`SPEC-SELF-RELEASE-LIFECYCLE`](projects/SPEC-SELF-RELEASE-LIFECYCLE.json).
+
+## Authority
+
+A verified merge of a managed Callisto release PR is the sole authorization for publication.
+There is no GitHub Environment reviewer, deployment protection gate, or second manual click.
+Merge evidence and release authorization are separate concerns: required CI checks protect the
+merge; the merge authorizes the release.
+
+## Release identity and recovery
+
+Every release run records two different revisions:
+
+- The orchestration revision: the workflow and Callisto CLI that coordinate the run.
+- The release-source revision: the merged release commit whose exact versions are released.
+
+A recovery is a new run using current orchestration and an explicit full release-source SHA. It
+does not rerun historical workflow code, create a version PR, or invent a newer version.
+
+The immutable run envelope and provider observations are recovery authority. A local state file
+is useful crash evidence, but cannot prove what a registry, Git remote, or forge contains.
+
+## Execution
+
+Before an effect, Callisto observes the provider. An operation is one of absent, exact success,
+conflict, or indeterminate. Exact success becomes `AlreadySatisfied`; Callisto must not publish
+the same version merely to learn whether it exists. Conflict and indeterminate observations fail
+closed with an actionable diagnostic.
+
+The release succeeds only when every operation is provider-observed as exact success or already
+satisfied. `Attempting`, failed, blocked, missing, and indeterminate are non-success states. A
+receipt is emitted only after that global condition holds.
+
+## Workflow boundary
+
+GitHub Actions schedules jobs, supplies two isolated checkouts, transports artifacts, and injects
+credentials only into execute. Callisto owns source validation, provenance, plan derivation,
+provider observation, transition selection, resume, terminality, receipt creation, and artifact
+validation. Workflow shell must not reimplement those semantics.
+
+All transient intent, state, downloaded artifacts, and build output live under `RUNNER_TEMP`, not
+inside a source checkout. Build and plan have no registry credentials or provider-write token.
+
+## Product assets and rehearsal
+
+The product release will contain attested assets for `aarch64-apple-darwin`,
+`x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, and `wasm32-wasip1`. Apple signing and
+notarization are intentionally out of scope until the project has a safe project-owned policy.
+
+The private `orin-dx/callisto-rehearsal` forge repository is isolated from production. It is not,
+by itself, an end-to-end rehearsal: each registry needs a real isolated destination and
+credentials. The workflow must fail closed when that infrastructure is not provisioned.
